question: What are the two landing requirements for a multi-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: A landing climb requirement and a tyre speed requirement
A landing distance requirement and a landing climb requirement
A landing distance requirement and a brake energy requirement

explanation: The aeroplane must be able to land within the required distance, and if it cannot land, it must be able to climb away with an adequate gradient.

question: What is the maximum mass that still meets the landing climb gradients called?
explanation: The landing climb limit mass is the greatest mass at which the minimum landing climb gradients can still be achieved.

question: What all-engines baulked landing gradient is required of a multi-engine Class B aeroplane?
explanation: With all engines operating, the steady climb gradient in the landing configuration must be at least 2.5%.

question: For the all-engines baulked landing requirement, what power is used?

options.text: The power needed for level flight at VREF in the landing configuration

explanation: The engines are at the power developed 8 seconds after the power levers are moved to the take-off position, allowing for spool-up.

question: In what configuration is the all-engines baulked landing gradient demonstrated?

options.text: Gear down, take-off flap, speed V2 plus 10 kt
Gear down, landing flap, speed VREF
Gear up, landing flap, speed VREF
Gear up, flaps up, speed 1.2 VS1

explanation: For the baulked landing the gear is extended and flaps are at the landing setting, at a climb speed equal to VREF.

question: What one-engine-inoperative missed approach gradient is required of a multi-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: At least 0.75% at 1 500 ft above the landing surface

explanation: With the critical engine inoperative, the gradient must be at least 0.75% at 1 500 ft above the landing surface.

question: In what configuration is the one-engine-inoperative missed approach gradient demonstrated?

options.text: Gear down, flaps up, propeller windmilling
Gear down, landing flap, live engine at take-off power, propeller windmilling
Gear up, approach flap, both engines at idle
Gear and flaps up, propeller feathered, live engine at MCP

explanation: The critical engine is inoperative with its propeller feathered, the live engine at maximum continuous power, gear and flaps retracted, and a speed of at least 1.2 VS1.

question: What climb speed is assumed for the one-engine-inoperative missed approach requirement?
explanation: The climb speed must be not less than 1.2 VS1.

question: Why is the one-engine-inoperative missed approach gradient so much lower than the all-engines value?

options.text: The aeroplane is lighter when it lands
The missed approach is flown at a higher speed than the approach itself
Losing an engine costs about 75% of gradient

explanation: Losing an engine costs roughly three quarters of the climb gradient. A higher requirement would severely limit the payload.

question: To which multi-engine Class B aeroplanes do these specific landing climb gradients apply?

options.text: Normal, utility, aerobatic types over 2 722 kg

explanation: The gradients quoted (2.5% all engines, 0.75% one engine) apply to normal, utility and aerobatic category aeroplanes of more than 2 722 kg.

question: A landing climb chart gives a rate of climb rather than a gradient. What must be done to check the 2.5% requirement?

options.text: Nothing; the chart already shows compliance
Convert the rate of climb into a gradient
Multiply the rate of climb by 2.5
Compare the rate of climb directly with 250 ft/min

explanation: Gradient = rate of climb ÷ ground speed (in the same units) × 100.

question: A baulked landing chart gives 700 ft/min at 90 kt. What is the gradient, and does it meet the requirement?
A baulked landing gives 250 ft/min at 100 kt. Does it meet the all-engines requirement?

options.text: Yes; about 2.5%, which just meets it

explanation: 100 kt ≈ 10 133 ft/min; 250 ÷ 10 133 × 100 ≈ 2.47%, slightly below 2.5%, so the mass must be reduced.

question: What landing distance requirement applies to a multi-engine Class B aeroplane?

options.text: A full stop from 50 ft within 70% of the LDA
A full stop from 50 ft within 85% of the LDA
A full stop from 35 ft within the LDA
A full stop from 50 ft within 60% of the LDA

explanation: As for single-engine Class B, the landing must be completed from 50 ft within 70% of the LDA at destination and alternates (factor 1.43).

question: The gross landing distance of a light twin is 2 100 ft. What is the shortest acceptable LDA?
A light twin will land on a grass runway (firm soil, short grass) that may be wet. What factor applies for the wet condition?

options.text: 1.0, because the grass factor already covers a wet surface
1.15, as well as the grass factor

explanation: Both corrections are applied: 1.15 for grass and 1.15 if the runway may be wet, unless the manual gives specific wet data.

question: Which slope correction applies to a light twin's landing distance?

options.text: No slope correction at all for multi-engine aeroplanes

explanation: The same rule as for singles: +5% per 1% downslope and no credit for upslope.

question: Besides 1.3 VS0, which speed must a light twin's VREF also exceed?
explanation: A twin must also be above the landing minimum control speed, VMCL, so it can be controlled if an engine fails during the approach.

question: What are the despatch rules for a light twin's landing?

options.text: The same as for single-engine Class B
Two alternates must always be planned
Only the runway into wind need be considered at the destination

explanation: As for singles, both assumptions apply, and if the forecast-wind case cannot be met an alternate with full compliance must be designated.

question: Why should short summaries of the performance rules be treated with care?

options.text: They are always out of date
They summarise the full rules and may omit detail
They include the safety factors twice over in some places
They apply only to single-engine aeroplanes

explanation: Summaries give very abbreviated versions of the requirements and may be misleading if read as the complete rule.
